skills.conservation: Name the conserved quantity and its condition
skills.graphs: Graphs and what slope or area means

prompts.title: What a straight position graph says
prompts.context: A cart moves along a straight track. Its position-time graph is a straight line from x = 2.0 m at t = 0 to x = 10.0 m at t = 4.0 s.
prompts.prompt: Determine the cart's velocity, and justify whether the cart is speeding up.
checklist: Uses the slope of the position-time graph as the velocity: (10.0 m − 2.0 m) / 4.0 s = 2.0 m/s
Says the slope is the same everywhere because the graph is a straight line
Concludes the velocity is constant, so the acceleration is zero and the cart is not speeding up

earns.answer: The velocity is the slope of the position-time graph: (10.0 m − 2.0 m) / (4.0 s − 0) = 2.0 m/s. The graph is a straight line, so its slope, and with it the velocity, is the same at every instant. A constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the cart is not speeding up even though its position keeps increasing.
earns.why: It reads the right feature of the graph (the slope, not the height), gives the value with its unit, and links a constant slope to a constant velocity.

misses.answer: The cart is speeding up, because its position keeps getting larger as time goes on.
misses.why: A growing position only means the cart moves forward. Speeding up would need a slope that gets steeper; this answer reads the height of the graph instead of its slope.

prompts.title: Displacement from a velocity graph
prompts.context: A runner starts from rest. Her velocity-time graph rises in a straight line from 0 to 6.0 m/s over the first 3.0 s, then stays flat at 6.0 m/s from 3.0 s to 6.0 s.
prompts.prompt: Calculate her displacement from t = 0 to t = 6.0 s, and explain how you used the graph.
checklist: Uses the area between the velocity-time graph and the time axis as the displacement
Splits the area into a triangle, ½(3.0 s)(6.0 m/s) = 9.0 m, and a rectangle, (3.0 s)(6.0 m/s) = 18 m
Adds them: 27 m, with the unit

earns.answer: The displacement is the area between the velocity-time graph and the time axis. From 0 to 3.0 s the area is a triangle, ½(3.0 s)(6.0 m/s) = 9.0 m. From 3.0 s to 6.0 s it is a rectangle, (3.0 s)(6.0 m/s) = 18 m. The displacement is 9.0 m + 18 m = 27 m.
earns.why: It names the graph feature (area), handles the part where the velocity is changing, and gives a value with its unit.

misses.answer: Displacement = velocity × time = (6.0 m/s)(6.0 s) = 36 m.
misses.why: This treats the velocity as 6.0 m/s the whole time. During the first 3.0 s she is slower than that, so the area under the rising part is a triangle, not a rectangle.

prompts.title: Measure a cart's acceleration
prompts.context: You have a cart, a long ramp, a meterstick, a stopwatch and tape for marking the ramp. The cart is released from rest and speeds up with constant acceleration down the ramp.
prompts.prompt: Describe a procedure to find the cart's acceleration, including what you would graph and how you would use the graph.
checklist: Releases the cart from rest at a marked start, with the meterstick measuring the distance d to several finish marks
Times each run with the stopwatch, repeating each distance several times and averaging to reduce uncertainty
Graphs d against t² (from d = ½at² for a start from rest), draws a best-fit straight line, and uses a = 2 × slope

earns.answer: Mark a start line and five finish lines at different distances d down the ramp, measuring each d with the meterstick. Release the cart from rest at the start line and time how long it takes to reach a finish line with the stopwatch; do three trials for each distance and average the times. Because the cart starts from rest with constant acceleration, d = ½at². So graph d (vertical) against t² (horizontal), draw the best-fit straight line, and find its slope: the slope is a/2, so a = 2 × slope.
earns.why: It names each measured quantity with its instrument, repeats trials, chooses a graph that is a straight line, and says how its slope gives the acceleration.

misses.answer: Roll the cart down the ramp and time it with the stopwatch. Then the acceleration is a = v/t.
misses.why: It never says what distance is measured or how, uses one run, and v is not measured at all. The readers want measured quantities, instruments, repeats and how the graph gives the answer.

prompts.title: Which ball lands first
prompts.context: From the same height above level ground, at the same instant, one ball is dropped from rest and an identical ball is launched horizontally at 8.0 m/s. Air resistance is negligible.
prompts.prompt: Predict which ball reaches the ground first, and justify your prediction.
checklist: Claims they land at the same time
Says the horizontal and vertical motions are independent, so the horizontal speed does not change the vertical motion
Both start with zero vertical velocity, have the same downward acceleration g and fall the same height, so h = ½gt² gives the same t = √(2h/g) for both

earns.answer: They land at the same time. The horizontal and vertical motions of a projectile are independent. Vertically, both balls start with zero velocity, both have the same downward acceleration g, and both fall the same height h, so h = ½gt² gives the same time t = √(2h/g) for each. The launched ball's 8.0 m/s horizontal velocity does not appear in this equation; it only carries that ball farther from the starting point.
earns.why: It makes the claim, names the independence of the two motions, and shows from the vertical equation that the horizontal speed cannot change the time.

misses.answer: The dropped ball lands first, because it travels a shorter distance than the ball that moves sideways.
misses.why: The time to land depends only on the vertical motion. The launched ball does go farther, but sideways, and that does not slow its fall.

prompts.title: Who pushes harder in a crash
prompts.context: A small car runs head-on into a large truck. A student says the truck exerts a larger force on the car than the car exerts on the truck, because the car is damaged more and slows down more.
prompts.prompt: Evaluate the student's claim and justify your answer.
checklist: States the claim is wrong: the two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction
Names them as a Newton's third law pair: the force of the truck on the car and the force of the car on the truck, from one interaction
Explains the different effects with a = F/m: the same size of force gives the smaller-mass car the larger acceleration

earns.answer: The claim is wrong. The force of the truck on the car and the force of the car on the truck are the two forces of one interaction, so by Newton's third law they are equal in size and opposite in direction. The car changes velocity more because of Newton's second law: the same size of force on a smaller mass gives a larger acceleration, a = F/m.
earns.why: It names the third-law pair (who exerts each force on whom) and explains the different outcomes with the second law instead of with different forces.

misses.answer: The truck pushes harder because it is heavier, so the car is pushed back more.
misses.why: Mass does not change the size of the forces in an interaction pair. This answer mixes up the size of the force with the size of its effect.

prompts.title: Tension in an elevator that slows down
prompts.context: An elevator car is moving upward and slowing down as it approaches a floor. A student says the cable's tension must be larger than the car's weight, since the car is going up.
prompts.prompt: Evaluate the student's claim using the forces on the car, and justify your answer.
checklist: States the claim is wrong: the tension is smaller than the weight
Says the car moves up but slows down, so its acceleration points down
Uses Newton's second law: the net force points the same way as the acceleration, so the downward gravitational force is larger than the upward tension

earns.answer: The claim is wrong; the tension is smaller than the car's weight. Two forces act on the car: the cable's tension up and the gravitational force of Earth down. The car moves upward but is slowing down, so its acceleration points down. By Newton's second law the net force points the same way as the acceleration, down, so the downward gravitational force is larger than the upward tension.
earns.why: It separates velocity (up) from acceleration (down) and links the direction of the net force to the acceleration, not to the motion.

misses.answer: The tension is bigger than the weight, because the elevator is still moving up and something has to keep it moving.
misses.why: This links the forces to the direction of motion. The net force sets the acceleration; an object moving up can have a net force down while it slows.

prompts.title: Double the hanging mass
prompts.context: A 2.0 kg cart on a level, frictionless track is pulled by a light string over an ideal pulley to a hanging 0.50 kg block. A student doubles the hanging mass to 1.0 kg and predicts the acceleration will double. Use g = 9.8 m/s².
prompts.prompt: Derive an expression for the acceleration, and use it to evaluate the student's prediction.
checklist: Takes the cart, string and block as one system: the unbalanced external force is the hanging block's weight, mg
Writes a = mg/(M + m), with M the cart's mass and m the hanging mass
Shows the acceleration rises from 1.96 m/s² to 3.27 m/s², less than double, because the total mass being accelerated also grows

earns.answer: Take the cart, the string and the hanging block as the system. The only unbalanced external force along the motion is the block's weight, mg, and it accelerates the whole mass M + m, so a = mg/(M + m). With m = 0.50 kg, a = (0.50)(9.8)/(2.50) = 1.96 m/s². With m = 1.0 kg, a = (1.0)(9.8)/(3.0) = 3.27 m/s². The acceleration does not double: doubling m doubles the pulling force, but it also increases the total mass the force must accelerate.
earns.why: It derives the dependence from Newton's second law for a named system and reads it correctly: m appears on the top and the bottom.

misses.answer: Yes, it doubles. F = ma, so twice the hanging weight gives twice the acceleration.
misses.why: The doubled force acts on a larger total mass. Reading "twice the force, twice the acceleration" holds only when the mass stays the same.

prompts.title: Is the normal force equal to the weight?
prompts.context: A 5.0 kg box rests on a ramp tilted 30° above the horizontal. Static friction keeps it from sliding. Use g = 9.8 m/s².
prompts.prompt: Compare the normal force of the ramp on the box with the box's weight, and justify your answer.
checklist: Claims the normal force is smaller than the weight: F_N = mg cos 30° = 42 N, while mg = 49 N
Says the normal force is perpendicular to the ramp surface, so only forces perpendicular to the surface balance it
Says the box is at rest, so forces balance along each axis: perpendicular, F_N balances the part of the gravitational force into the ramp; along it, static friction balances the part down the slope

earns.answer: The normal force is smaller than the weight. The box is at rest, so the net force on it is zero along each axis. Take axes along and perpendicular to the ramp. The normal force of the ramp on the box is perpendicular to the surface, so it balances only the part of the gravitational force pressing into the ramp: F_N = mg cos 30° = (5.0 kg)(9.8 m/s²)(0.866) = 42 N, less than mg = 49 N. The part of the gravitational force down the slope is balanced by static friction.
earns.why: It uses the direction of the normal force and the equilibrium condition along each axis, and gets a number to back the comparison.

misses.answer: The normal force equals the weight, 49 N, because the box is not moving.
misses.why: Being at rest means all the forces balance, not that the normal force alone balances the weight. On a slope, friction does part of the job, so the normal force is smaller.

prompts.title: The forces at the top of a loop
prompts.context: A roller-coaster car moves along the inside of a vertical circular loop. At the very top it is upside down and moving fast enough to stay on the track.
prompts.prompt: Identify every force on the car at the top, and explain why no separate centripetal force belongs on its free-body diagram.
checklist: Names two forces, both pointing down: the gravitational force of Earth on the car and the normal force of the track on the car
Says the track is above the car at the top, so its push points down, toward the center
Says the centripetal net force is the sum of these real forces (F_g + F_N = mv²/r), not an extra force, so drawing it would count it twice

earns.answer: Two forces act on the car at the top: the gravitational force of Earth on the car, down, and the normal force of the track on the car, also down, because the track is above the car and pushes it toward the center of the loop. Their sum is the centripetal net force, F_g + F_N = mv²/r, pointing to the center. "Centripetal force" is a name for that net force, not a separate push or pull from some object, so drawing it as an extra arrow would count the same forces twice.
earns.why: It names each real force with its agent and direction and explains what "centripetal" means: the net force, not a new force.

misses.answer: Gravity pulls down, the normal force pushes up, and the centripetal force points down toward the center.
misses.why: At the top of the inside of a loop, the track pushes down, not up. And the centripetal force is not a third force: the readers mark an extra centripetal arrow as wrong.

prompts.title: Is the ball's mechanical energy conserved?
prompts.context: A ball is dropped from rest and falls 2.0 m. Air resistance is negligible. One student says its mechanical energy is conserved; another says its kinetic energy increases, so energy is not conserved.
prompts.prompt: Explain how both students can be partly right, by naming the system each is using.
checklist: Names the ball-Earth system: only the internal gravitational force does work and no external force does work, so K + U_g stays constant
Names the ball-alone system: there is no potential energy, and Earth's gravitational force is external and does positive work, so the ball's K increases
Says whether energy is constant depends on the system chosen, not on a rule that energy is always constant

earns.answer: It depends on the system. For the ball-Earth system, the gravitational force is internal, no external force does work and air resistance is negligible, so the mechanical energy K + U_g stays constant: U_g decreases by mg(2.0 m) and K increases by the same amount. For the ball alone there is no potential energy; Earth's gravitational force is an external force that does positive work, mg(2.0 m), on the ball, so the ball's kinetic energy increases. Both descriptions agree once the system is named.
earns.why: It names each system, says which forces are internal or external, and gives the condition (no external work) that makes the energy constant.

misses.answer: Mechanical energy is conserved because energy is always conserved; it can never be created or destroyed.
misses.why: Energy is conserved overall, but the mechanical energy of a chosen system stays constant only when no external work is done and no energy is converted to thermal energy. This names no system and no condition.

prompts.title: Where the missing speed went
prompts.context: A block slides from rest down a rough ramp from a height h. At the bottom its speed is less than √(2gh), the speed it would have on a frictionless ramp.
prompts.prompt: Explain why, using the energy of a named system.
checklist: Names a system, the block, the ramp and Earth, and says kinetic friction acts between block and ramp as the block slides
Says kinetic friction converts some of the mechanical energy into thermal energy of the block and ramp
Writes the energy balance mgh = ½mv² + (thermal energy), so ½mv² is less than mgh and v is less than √(2gh)

earns.answer: Take the block, the ramp and Earth as the system. As the block slides, kinetic friction between the block and the ramp converts some of the system's mechanical energy into thermal energy of the block and ramp surfaces. So mgh = ½mv² + E_thermal, where E_thermal = f_k d for a slide of length d. The kinetic energy at the bottom is less than mgh, so the speed is less than √(2gh).
earns.why: It names the system, the process (kinetic friction) and where the energy goes (thermal energy), and shows the effect in the energy equation.

misses.answer: The block has less speed because some energy is lost to friction on the way down.
misses.why: Energy is not lost: it becomes thermal energy of the surfaces. The readers ask where the energy goes and in which system, and this answer names neither.

prompts.title: The shape of the total energy graph
prompts.context: A skater glides along a frictionless track that dips down into a valley and rises over a hill. You are asked to sketch K, U_g and the total mechanical energy of the skater-Earth system against the skater's horizontal position.
prompts.prompt: Describe the shape of the total mechanical energy graph, and justify it.
checklist: Says the total is a horizontal line at the same value at every position
Justifies it: no friction and no external work on the skater-Earth system, so K + U_g does not change
Says K and U_g mirror each other: where U_g dips (the valley), K rises by the same amount

earns.answer: The total mechanical energy graph is a horizontal line. The track is frictionless and no external force does work on the skater-Earth system, so K + U_g has the same value at every position. The other two graphs mirror each other: U_g follows the shape of the track, lowest in the valley, and K is largest in the valley, so that their sum stays flat.
earns.why: It gives the shape, the condition that makes it flat, and how the two other graphs combine to give it.

misses.answer: The total energy goes down into the valley and back up over the hill, following the track.
misses.why: This describes U_g, not the total. The readers often see a sloping or curved total line; with no friction and no external work it must be flat.

prompts.title: Two motors, one load
prompts.context: Two motors each lift an identical 20 kg crate 3.0 m straight up at constant speed. Motor A takes 6.0 s and motor B takes 3.0 s.
prompts.prompt: Compare the work done and the average power of the two motors, and justify each comparison.
checklist: Says each motor does the same work, mgh = (20 kg)(9.8 m/s²)(3.0 m) = 588 J, because the mass and height are the same and the speed is constant
Uses P = W/Δt: the same work in half the time means twice the average power
Gives the values: motor A 98 W, motor B 196 W

earns.answer: They do the same work. Each crate rises at constant speed, so the motor's force equals the crate's weight and the work is W = mgh = (20 kg)(9.8 m/s²)(3.0 m) = 588 J for both. Average power is work divided by time, P = W/Δt. Motor B does the same work in half the time, so its average power is twice motor A's: 196 W for B and 98 W for A.
earns.why: It separates work (depends on force and distance) from power (work per unit time) and gives the factor with numbers.

misses.answer: Motor B does more work because it is faster, so it has more power.
misses.why: Both motors do the same work, since the force and distance are the same. Speed changes how fast the work is done, which is the power, not the work.

prompts.title: Impulse from a force-time graph
prompts.context: A bat hits a 0.050 kg ball at rest. A force sensor shows the force on the ball rising in a straight line from 0 to 400 N and back to 0, in the shape of a triangle that lasts 0.010 s.
prompts.prompt: Calculate the ball's speed just after the hit, and explain how you used the graph.
checklist: Uses the area under the force-time graph as the impulse on the ball
Finds the triangle's area: ½(400 N)(0.010 s) = 2.0 N·s
Uses impulse = change in momentum: 2.0 N·s = (0.050 kg)v, so v = 40 m/s

earns.answer: The impulse on the ball is the area under the force-time graph. The graph is a triangle, so J = ½(400 N)(0.010 s) = 2.0 N·s. By the impulse-momentum theorem, the impulse equals the ball's change in momentum: 2.0 N·s = (0.050 kg)(v − 0), so v = 40 m/s.
earns.why: It names the graph feature (area), handles the changing force correctly, and links impulse to the change in momentum.

misses.why: This uses the peak force as if it lasted the whole 0.010 s. The force changes, so the impulse is the area of the triangle, half of this.

prompts.title: Why the skaters' momentum stays zero
prompts.context: Two skaters stand at rest on smooth ice and push off each other. Afterward they glide apart in opposite directions.
prompts.prompt: Justify the claim that the total momentum of the two skaters is zero after they separate.
checklist: Names the system: both skaters together
Says the pushes are internal forces, a third-law pair, equal in size and opposite in direction
Says the external forces (gravity and the ice's normal force) balance and ice friction is negligible, so the net external force is zero and the total momentum stays zero, its value before the push

earns.answer: Take the two skaters as the system. The pushes they exert on each other are internal forces, a Newton's third law pair, equal in size and opposite in direction, so they cannot change the system's total momentum. The external forces on the system, the gravitational force of Earth and the normal force of the ice, are vertical and balance, and friction from the smooth ice is negligible. With zero net external force, the total momentum stays at its initial value, zero, so afterward the skaters' momenta are equal in size and opposite in direction.
earns.why: It names the system and gives the condition (zero net external force) instead of quoting the law.

misses.answer: The total momentum is zero because momentum is conserved because of the law of conservation of momentum.
misses.why: This is circular: it names the law but not why it applies here. The readers give the point only when the answer says the net external force on the system is zero.

prompts.title: Friction between a block and a cart
prompts.context: A block slides onto a cart that rests on a frictionless track. Friction between the block and the cart slows the block and speeds up the cart until they move together.
prompts.prompt: Determine whether the momentum of the block-cart system stays constant while they slide, and justify your answer.
checklist: Claims the total momentum of the block-cart system stays constant
Says friction between block and cart is internal: the cart's backward friction on the block and the block's forward friction on the cart are a third-law pair

Says the external forces are vertical and balance and the track is frictionless, so the net external horizontal force is zero; the block's own momentum does change, because for the block alone friction is external

earns.answer: Yes, it stays constant. Friction acts between the block and the cart: the cart pushes backward on the block and the block pushes forward on the cart, a third-law pair of equal size, so both are internal to the block-cart system. The external forces, the gravitational forces and the track's normal force, are vertical and balance, and the track is frictionless, so the net external horizontal force is zero and the total momentum is constant. The block's own momentum does decrease, because for the block alone the cart's friction is an external force.
earns.why: It links the word "internal" to the reason it matters (a third-law pair cancels in the system) and states the condition for the system.

misses.answer: No. Friction always takes momentum away, so the momentum decreases while they slide.
misses.why: Friction removes kinetic energy here, not momentum. What matters for momentum is whether a force is external to the chosen system, and this friction is internal.

prompts.title: Momentum first in a sticky collision
prompts.context: A 0.20 kg lump of clay moving at 5.0 m/s hits a 0.80 kg cart at rest on a level, low-friction track and sticks to it. A student finds the speed afterward by setting the kinetic energy before equal to the kinetic energy after.
prompts.prompt: Explain why the student's method is wrong, and calculate the speed after the collision correctly.
checklist: Says the net external force on the clay-cart system is negligible during the collision, so its momentum is the same before and after
Says kinetic energy is not conserved when the objects stick: some becomes thermal energy and deformation
Calculates v = (0.20 kg)(5.0 m/s) / (1.00 kg) = 1.0 m/s, and shows the kinetic energy falls from 2.5 J to 0.50 J

earns.answer: Take the clay and the cart as the system. During the collision the net external force on it is negligible (the vertical forces balance and the track has little friction), so its total momentum is the same before and after: (0.20 kg)(5.0 m/s) = (1.00 kg)v, so v = 1.0 m/s. Kinetic energy is not conserved in a collision where the objects stick: it falls from ½(0.20)(5.0)² = 2.5 J to ½(1.00)(1.0)² = 0.50 J, the rest becoming thermal energy and deformation of the clay. So the student's equation is false.
earns.why: It starts from momentum with its condition, explains why kinetic energy cannot be used, and backs both with numbers.

misses.answer: Kinetic energy before = kinetic energy after: ½(0.20)(5.0)² = ½(1.00)v², so v = 2.2 m/s.
misses.why: This is the error the readers report most in this kind of question: in a sticky (perfectly inelastic) collision kinetic energy is not conserved, so this equation gives the wrong speed.

prompts.title: Same mass, different spin-up
prompts.context: Two rods have the same length and the same total mass, and each turns about an axis through its center. Rod A has most of its mass in two heavy caps at its ends; rod B has most of its mass in a heavy sleeve at its center. The same net torque acts on each, starting from rest.
prompts.prompt: Predict which rod has the greater angular acceleration, and justify your prediction.
checklist: Claims rod B has the greater angular acceleration
Uses I = Σmr²: the same mass farther from the axis gives a larger rotational inertia, so rod A has the larger I
Uses Newton's second law in rotational form, α = τ/I: with the same torque, the smaller I gives the larger α

earns.answer: Rod B speeds up faster. The rotational inertia I = Σmr² depends on how far each bit of mass is from the axis, squared. Rod A has its mass far from the axis, so its I is larger; rod B has its mass near the axis, so its I is smaller. By Newton's second law in rotational form, α = τ/I, the same net torque gives the rod with the smaller rotational inertia, B, the larger angular acceleration.
earns.why: It explains the difference in I from the distribution of mass (r², not m alone) and then uses τ = Iα.

misses.answer: They have the same angular acceleration, because they have the same mass and the same torque.
misses.why: For rotation the mass alone does not set the response; where the mass sits does. Equal masses can have very different rotational inertias.

prompts.title: How hard you lift a wheelbarrow
prompts.context: A gardener holds a loaded wheelbarrow at rest with its handles lifted, so its legs are just off the ground. The 420 N load sits 0.50 m (measured horizontally) from the wheel's axle, the wheelbarrow's own 140 N weight acts 0.60 m from the axle, and her hands lift straight up on the handles 1.40 m from the axle. A friend says she must lift 560 N, the total weight.
prompts.prompt: Evaluate the friend's claim, and justify your answer with a calculation.
checklist: Takes torques about the wheel's axle, so the ground's unknown force on the wheel has no lever arm and no torque
Uses rotational equilibrium: the torque of the lift about the axle balances the torques of the load and of the wheelbarrow's weight
Solves F(1.40 m) = (420 N)(0.50 m) + (140 N)(0.60 m), so F = 210 N, less than 560 N; the ground pushes up on the wheel with the remaining 350 N

earns.answer: The claim is wrong. The wheelbarrow is at rest, so the net torque about any axis is zero. Taking the wheel's axle as the axis removes the ground's unknown force on the wheel, which has no lever arm there. The upward lift at 1.40 m must balance the torques of the load at 0.50 m and of the wheelbarrow's weight at 0.60 m: F(1.40 m) = (420 N)(0.50 m) + (140 N)(0.60 m) = 294 N·m, so F = 210 N. The net force is zero too, so the ground pushes up on the wheel with 560 N − 210 N = 350 N. Her lift is smaller than the total weight because it acts much farther from the axle.
earns.why: It picks a sensible axis, includes the wheelbarrow's own weight, balances torques, and checks the forces add up.

misses.answer: She must lift the whole weight, 420 N + 140 N = 560 N, because she is holding everything up.
misses.why: She is not the only one holding it up: the ground pushes on the wheel. Her lift is set by balancing torques about the axle, so the lever arms matter, the error the readers report when a force is assumed to equal a weight.

prompts.title: Tension on a pulley with mass
prompts.context: A block of mass m hangs from a string wrapped around a pulley with mass, which turns on a frictionless axle. The block is released from rest and falls while the pulley spins up.
prompts.prompt: Compare the string's tension with the block's weight mg while the block falls, and justify your answer using the block and the pulley.
checklist: Claims the tension is less than mg
For the block: it speeds up downward, so the net force on it is down: mg − T = ma with a greater than 0, so T is less than mg
For the pulley: the tension is what gives it a net torque TR = Iα, so T is greater than zero; the tension is between 0 and mg

earns.answer: The tension is less than mg. The block speeds up downward, so the net force on it points down: mg − T = ma, with a greater than zero, so T is less than mg. The tension is not zero either: it is the only force with a torque about the pulley's axle, and that torque, TR = Iα, is what spins the pulley up. So 0 is less than T, which is less than mg.
earns.why: It uses Newton's second law for the block and the rotational form for the pulley, and ties each to the direction of motion.

misses.answer: The tension equals mg, because the string is holding the block.
misses.why: The string would hold up the full weight only if the block were at rest or moving at constant velocity. The block accelerates down, so the net force on it is not zero.

prompts.title: Rotational inertia from a slope
prompts.context: A student applies several steady torques to a wheel on a low-friction axle and measures its angular acceleration. Her data: 0.40 N·m gives 2.0 rad/s², 0.80 N·m gives 4.1 rad/s², 1.20 N·m gives 6.0 rad/s². She graphs torque (vertical) against angular acceleration (horizontal).
prompts.prompt: Explain what the slope of her graph represents, and determine the wheel's rotational inertia from it.
checklist: Uses Newton's second law in rotational form, τ = Iα, so the graph of τ against α is a straight line through the origin whose slope is I
Draws a best-fit line through the data rather than using one data point or connecting the dots
Finds the slope from two points on the best-fit line, far apart, (1.20 − 0.40) N·m / (6.0 − 2.0) rad/s² = 0.20 kg·m², with the unit

earns.answer: Newton's second law for rotation says τ = Iα, so a graph of τ against α is a straight line through the origin whose slope is the rotational inertia I. Draw the best-fit line through the three points rather than using any one point. Read two points on the line itself, far apart; here the line passes almost exactly through (2.0 rad/s², 0.40 N·m) and (6.0 rad/s², 1.20 N·m), so its slope is (1.20 N·m − 0.40 N·m) / (6.0 rad/s² − 2.0 rad/s²) = 0.20 kg·m². So the wheel's rotational inertia is 0.20 kg·m².
earns.why: It names what the slope means from the equation, uses the best-fit line, and gives the value with its unit.

misses.answer: I = τ/α = 1.20/6.0 = 0.20 for the last trial, so the slope is 0.20.
misses.why: One trial is not the slope of the graph, and the value has no unit. The point of plotting is to use every trial through a best-fit line; with scattered data one point can be well off the line.

prompts.title: Why the spinning skater speeds up
prompts.context: A skater spins on smooth ice with her arms out, then pulls her arms in and spins faster.
prompts.prompt: Explain why her angular velocity increases, and determine whether her rotational kinetic energy stays the same.
checklist: Names the system, the skater, and says the net external torque about her vertical axis is zero: the ice is smooth, and gravity and the normal force have no lever arm about that axis
Says her angular momentum L = Iω is constant, so pulling her arms in (smaller I) makes ω larger
Says her rotational kinetic energy ½Iω² = L²/(2I) increases, because her muscles do positive work pulling her arms in

earns.answer: Take the skater as the system. The ice is smooth, and the gravitational and normal forces act along her vertical axis, so they have no lever arm and the net external torque about that axis is zero. Her angular momentum, L = Iω, therefore stays constant. Pulling her arms in moves mass closer to the axis and makes I smaller, so ω must increase. Her rotational kinetic energy, ½Iω² = L²/(2I), increases as I decreases: her muscles do positive work on her arms as she pulls them inward.
earns.why: It gives the condition (zero net external torque) before the conservation law, and does not confuse constant angular momentum with constant kinetic energy.

misses.answer: She spins faster because her energy is conserved, and with a smaller I she needs a bigger ω to keep the same energy.
misses.why: Her angular momentum is what stays constant; her kinetic energy increases. This mixes up the two conservation laws, as the readers report for collisions too.

prompts.title: What is conserved when a child jumps on
prompts.context: A child runs along a line tangent to the rim of a merry-go-round that turns freely on a fixed axle, and jumps on. The merry-go-round speeds up.
prompts.prompt: Explain which of these stays constant for the child-merry-go-round system during the jump: its linear momentum, its angular momentum about the axle, its kinetic energy.
checklist: Says angular momentum about the axle stays constant: the axle's force acts at the axis, so it has no lever arm, and the net external torque is zero
Says linear momentum does not stay constant: the axle exerts an external force that keeps the merry-go-round's center in place
Says kinetic energy decreases: the child and the rim end up moving together, like a perfectly inelastic collision

earns.answer: Only the angular momentum about the axle stays constant. The axle exerts an external force on the merry-go-round, so the system's linear momentum changes: the child's straight-line momentum does not carry on after the jump. But that axle force acts at the axis, where it has no lever arm, and friction at the axle is negligible, so the net external torque about the axle is zero and the angular momentum is constant. Kinetic energy is not constant: the child and the rim end up moving together, as in a perfectly inelastic collision, and some kinetic energy becomes thermal energy.
earns.why: It treats each quantity with its own condition: an external force can act with no external torque.

misses.answer: All three are conserved, because nothing outside the system pushes on it during the jump.
misses.why: The axle does push on the merry-go-round, so linear momentum is not conserved. And the child sticks to the rim, so kinetic energy is not conserved either.

prompts.title: Sphere against hoop
prompts.context: A solid sphere (I = ⅖MR²) and a hoop (I = MR²) of the same mass and radius are released together from rest at the top of a ramp and roll down without slipping.
prompts.prompt: Predict which reaches the bottom first, and justify your prediction using energy.
checklist: Uses the energy of each object with Earth: Mgh = ½Mv² + ½Iω², with v = Rω for rolling without slipping
Writes I = βMR² and gets v = √(2gh/(1 + β)), so the speed does not depend on M or R
Concludes the sphere (β = ⅖) has the larger speed at every height and wins; the hoop puts more of its energy into rotation

earns.answer: The sphere wins. For each object and Earth, the static friction of rolling does no work, so Mgh = ½Mv² + ½Iω², with v = Rω because it rolls without slipping. Writing I = βMR² gives Mgh = ½Mv²(1 + β), so v = √(2gh/(1 + β)), with no M or R left. The sphere has β = ⅖ and the hoop β = 1, so at every height the sphere moves faster: more of its energy goes into translation and less into rotation.
earns.why: It derives the speed from energy with v = Rω and reads the dependence, so the reason is in the rotational inertia, not the mass.

misses.answer: They tie, because energy is conserved and they start at the same height with the same mass.
misses.why: The same total energy is shared differently between translation and rotation. The hoop's larger rotational inertia takes a larger share, so less is left for its speed.

prompts.title: Faster near the planet
prompts.context: A satellite moves in an elliptical orbit around a planet. It is moving fastest at the point closest to the planet.
prompts.prompt: Justify this with a conservation law, naming the system and its condition.
checklist: Names the satellite-planet system: the gravitational force is internal, and no external force does work on it, so K + U_G is constant
Uses U_G = −GMm/r: closer to the planet U_G is more negative, so K, and the speed, is larger
Or: the gravitational force on the satellite points at the planet, so its torque about the planet is zero and rmv sinθ is constant; a smaller r at the closest point (θ = 90°) means a larger v

earns.answer: Take the satellite and the planet as the system. The gravitational force between them is internal and no external force does work, so the total energy K + U_G is constant, with U_G = −GMm/r. At the closest point r is smallest, so U_G is most negative and K must be largest: the satellite moves fastest there. The same result follows from angular momentum: the gravitational force on the satellite points at the planet, so it has no torque about the planet, and the satellite's angular momentum rmv sinθ is constant. At the closest point θ = 90° and r is smallest, so v is largest.
earns.why: It names the system and the condition for each conservation law, and uses the r-dependence to reach the claim.

misses.answer: It goes faster because gravity is stronger when it is closer to the planet.
misses.why: A stronger pull alone does not explain a larger speed; the force is perpendicular to the velocity at the closest point. The readers want a conservation law with its condition.

prompts.title: A bigger swing, the same period
prompts.context: A block on a horizontal spring is pulled 4.0 cm from equilibrium and released; it oscillates with period T. It is then pulled 8.0 cm and released.
prompts.prompt: Predict the new period, and justify your prediction.
checklist: Claims the period stays T
Uses T = 2π√(m/k), which contains neither the amplitude nor any distance

Explains physically: at twice the amplitude the block travels twice as far, but the restoring force, and so the acceleration, is twice as large at each point, so it moves faster and the time is the same

earns.answer: The period stays T. For a block on a spring, T = 2π√(m/k), which depends only on the mass and the spring constant, not on the amplitude. Physically, at twice the amplitude the block has twice as far to go, but the restoring force F = −kx is twice as large at each corresponding point, so its acceleration and its speed are twice as large too. The two effects cancel, and each cycle takes the same time; only the greatest speed doubles.
earns.why: It uses the period equation correctly and explains why the amplitude cancels, which is what "justify" asks for.

misses.answer: The period doubles, because the block has to travel twice as far each cycle.
misses.why: Twice the distance does not mean twice the time here, because the block also moves faster. Amplitude changing the period is a common misconception the course tests for.

prompts.title: A heavier bob on a pendulum
prompts.context: A student replaces a pendulum's 0.10 kg bob with a 0.40 kg bob of the same size, keeping the string length the same. She predicts the period will double, using T = 2π√(m/k).
prompts.prompt: Evaluate her prediction, and justify your answer.
checklist: Says the prediction is wrong: the period stays the same
Says T = 2π√(m/k) is for a block on a spring; a simple pendulum has T = 2π√(ℓ/g), which has no mass in it
Explains why: the restoring force on the bob (part of its weight, mg) grows with m, but so does the bob's inertia, so the acceleration does not depend on m

earns.answer: Her prediction is wrong; the period stays the same. T = 2π√(m/k) is the period of a block on a spring. For a simple pendulum, T = 2π√(ℓ/g), which depends on the length and on g, not on the mass. The restoring force on the bob comes from its weight, mg, so a heavier bob has a larger restoring force, but it also has more mass to accelerate; the two cancel, and the bob's motion is the same.
earns.why: It names the right model for the system and explains why mass drops out, rather than only quoting the formula.

misses.answer: The heavier bob is four times the mass, so with T = 2π√(m/k) the period becomes √4 = 2 times as long.
misses.why: This uses the spring formula for a pendulum, an error the readers report. A pendulum has no spring constant; its restoring force comes from gravity, which also grows with the mass.

prompts.title: Find g with a pendulum
prompts.context: You have a string, a small heavy bob, a meterstick, a stopwatch and a clamp stand. You want to measure g from the period of a pendulum.
prompts.prompt: Describe a procedure, what you would graph to get a straight line, and how you would find g from it.
checklist: Measures the length ℓ from the pivot to the center of the bob with the meterstick, for at least five different lengths
For each length, releases the bob at a small angle and times 10 full oscillations with the stopwatch, then divides by 10 (repeating to average), so a period is not mistaken for half a swing
Graphs T² against ℓ: from T = 2π√(ℓ/g), T² = (4π²/g)ℓ, so the best-fit line's slope is 4π²/g and g = 4π²/slope (for example, a slope of 4.0 s²/m gives g = 9.87 m/s²)

earns.answer: Set up five pendulums of different lengths, measuring each length ℓ from the pivot to the center of the bob with the meterstick. For each, pull the bob aside to a small angle (under about 15°), release it, and time 10 complete back-and-forth oscillations with the stopwatch; divide by 10 to get the period T, and repeat three times to average. Since T = 2π√(ℓ/g), T² = (4π²/g)ℓ, so a graph of T² against ℓ is a straight line through the origin with slope 4π²/g. Draw the best-fit line and use g = 4π²/slope; for example, a slope of 4.0 s²/m gives g = 9.87 m/s².
earns.why: It names the instruments and measured quantities, reduces timing uncertainty, chooses a linear graph and says how the slope gives g.

misses.answer: Time one swing of the pendulum and measure the string. Then g = 4π²ℓ/T².
misses.why: One timing of one swing has a large uncertainty, and "one swing" is often half a period. With no graph and no repeats, this does not earn the procedure or the analysis points.

prompts.title: Where the block moves fastest
prompts.context: A block oscillates on a horizontal spring with amplitude A on a frictionless surface. A student says the block moves fastest at the turning points, because that is where the spring force is largest.
prompts.prompt: Evaluate the claim using the energy of the block-spring system.
checklist: Says the claim is wrong: the block moves fastest at equilibrium (x = 0) and is at rest at the turning points
Says the block-spring system has no friction and no external work, so its total energy ½kA² is constant
Says at x = 0 the spring's potential energy is zero, so all of the energy is kinetic; at x = ±A it is all potential, so K = 0; a large force means a large acceleration, not a large speed

earns.answer: The claim is wrong. Take the block and the spring as the system: the surface is frictionless and no external force does work, so the total energy ½kA² is constant. At the turning points, x = ±A, all of that energy is the spring's potential energy ½kA², so the block's kinetic energy is zero and it is momentarily at rest. At equilibrium, x = 0, the spring's potential energy is zero, so all of the energy is kinetic and the speed is greatest. The large spring force at the turning points gives the largest acceleration there, not the largest speed.
earns.why: It names the system and condition, tracks how the energy is shared, and separates acceleration from speed.

misses.answer: The block is fastest at the ends, because the spring force is biggest there and pushes it hardest.
misses.why: This confuses acceleration with speed. Where the force is largest, the block is at rest and just turning around.

prompts.title: Reading a pressure-depth graph
prompts.context: A diver's gauge records the absolute pressure at several depths in a lake. The graph of pressure against depth is a straight line that crosses the pressure axis at 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa and has a slope of 1.0 × 10⁴ Pa/m. Use g = 9.8 m/s².
prompts.prompt: Explain what the intercept and the slope represent, and determine the density of the lake water.
checklist: Uses P = P₀ + ρgh, so the graph of P against depth h is a straight line
Says the intercept is P₀, the atmospheric pressure at the surface, and the slope is ρg
Finds ρ = slope/g = (1.0 × 10⁴ Pa/m)/(9.8 m/s²) = 1.0 × 10³ kg/m³, with the unit

earns.answer: The absolute pressure at depth h is P = P₀ + ρgh. So a graph of P against h is a straight line whose intercept, at h = 0, is P₀: the atmospheric pressure pushing on the lake surface, 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Its slope is ρg. So ρ = slope/g = (1.0 × 10⁴ Pa/m) / (9.8 m/s²) = 1.0 × 10³ kg/m³ (about 1020 kg/m³).
earns.why: It reads both features of the graph from the equation, including why the line does not start at zero, and finds ρ with its unit.

misses.answer: Pressure is proportional to depth, so at 10 m, ρ = P/(gh) = (2.0 × 10⁵)/(9.8 × 10) = 2.0 × 10³ kg/m³.
misses.why: Absolute pressure is not proportional to depth: the line has an intercept, the atmosphere's pressure. Ignoring it doubles the density here. The slope, not one point, gives ρg.

prompts.title: Floating higher in salt water
prompts.context: A wooden block floats at rest in fresh water. It is moved to salt water, which is denser, and floats at rest again.
prompts.prompt: Predict whether more or less of the block is under the surface in salt water, and justify your prediction.
checklist: Claims less of the block is under water in salt water
Says floating at rest means the buoyant force balances the block's weight, so the buoyant force is the same in both liquids
Uses F_b = ρ_fluid V_under g: the same F_b with a larger ρ_fluid needs a smaller submerged volume

earns.answer: Less of the block is under water in salt water. The block floats at rest in both, so the buoyant force balances its weight each time; its weight has not changed, so the buoyant force is the same in both liquids. The buoyant force is F_b = ρ_fluid V_under g. Salt water has a larger density, so the same buoyant force needs a smaller submerged volume V_under, and the block floats higher.
earns.why: It uses the equilibrium of two separate forces and reads the dependence on the fluid's density correctly.

misses.answer: The salt water is denser, so it pushes up harder on the block and the buoyant force is bigger.
misses.why: The buoyant force cannot be bigger: the block floats at rest in both, so it equals the block's weight each time. The readers report this "denser fluid pushes harder" reasoning.

prompts.title: How fast a stone sinks at first
prompts.context: A granite stone (density 2700 kg/m³) is released from rest under water (density 1000 kg/m³). Ignore the water's drag at this low speed. Use g = 9.8 m/s².
prompts.prompt: Derive an expression for the stone's acceleration, calculate it, and explain why it is less than g.
checklist: Names two forces: the gravitational force of Earth down, ρ_stone V g, and the buoyant force of the water up, ρ_water V g
Uses Newton's second law: ρ_stone V a = ρ_stone V g − ρ_water V g, so a = g(1 − ρ_water/ρ_stone)
Calculates a = (9.8 m/s²)(1 − 1000/2700) = 6.2 m/s², less than g because the buoyant force points up and partly balances the weight

earns.answer: Two forces act on the stone: the gravitational force of Earth, down, of size ρ_stone V g, and the buoyant force of the water, up, of size ρ_water V g, where V is the stone's volume. By Newton's second law, (ρ_stone V)a = ρ_stone V g − ρ_water V g, so a = g(1 − ρ_water/ρ_stone) = (9.8 m/s²)(1 − 1000/2700) = 6.2 m/s², downward. It is less than g because the buoyant force points up, opposite the gravitational force, and cancels part of it.
earns.why: It keeps gravity and buoyancy as two separate forces in opposite directions, starts from Newton's second law, and shows the result.

misses.answer: Only the buoyant force acts under water, pushing up, so a = F_b/m = (1000/2700)(9.8) = 3.6 m/s² up.
misses.why: This drops the gravitational force, the error the readers report most on buoyancy questions. Both forces act on the stone, in opposite directions.

prompts.title: A hole four times as deep
prompts.context: Water leaks from a small hole in the side of a wide open tank, a depth h below the water surface. A second tank has a hole at depth 4h. Water is an ideal fluid.
prompts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed of the water leaving a hole, and use it to compare the two jet speeds.
checklist: Applies Bernoulli's equation from the water surface to the hole: both are open to the air, so the pressures are equal (atmospheric)
Uses continuity to take the surface speed as about zero, because the tank is much wider than the hole
Gets ρgh = ½ρv², so v = √(2gh): the density cancels, and v ∝ √h, so the 4h hole gives twice the speed

earns.answer: Apply Bernoulli's equation along the flow from the water surface to the hole: P₁ + ρgy₁ + ½ρv₁² = P₂ + ρgy₂ + ½ρv₂². Both points are open to the air, so P₁ = P₂. The tank is much wider than the hole, so by continuity (A₁v₁ = A₂v₂) the surface moves very slowly: v₁ ≈ 0. That leaves ρgh = ½ρv², so v = √(2gh). The density cancels, and v is proportional to √h, so the hole at depth 4h gives a jet √4 = 2 times as fast.
earns.why: It starts from a named principle, states each simplification with its reason, and reads the square-root dependence correctly.

misses.answer: Four times the depth gives four times the pressure, so the water comes out four times as fast.
misses.why: The gauge pressure at the hole does grow 4 times, but it sets the jet's kinetic energy per volume, ½ρv², not its speed. The speed grows as √h, so it doubles.
